stem: A 3-year-old girl has had constant hunger since infancy and severe obesity. Serum leptin is very low for her body fat. Her parents are healthy, and are second cousins.
oneliner: 3F + relentless hunger since infancy + severe obesity + very low leptin + healthy second-cousin parents → which inheritance pattern?
ask: Which inheritance pattern is most likely?

whyNot.B: Would need an **affected parent** in each generation; both parents are healthy
whyNot.C: A girl would need an **affected father** and a carrier or affected mother; parents are healthy
whyNot.D: Mitochondrial traits pass through the mother to all her children and are usually multisystem; **second-cousin parents** point to a recessive trait
whyNot.E: Imprinting on chromosome 15 gives Prader-Willi syndrome, with hypotonia and **high leptin**, not **very low leptin**

why: **Healthy related parents** and an affected child fit **autosomal recessive** inheritance, with both parents carrying a LEP mutation. With no leptin signal the brain senses starvation, causing **severe early hyperphagic obesity** that responds to leptin injections.

idea.rule: Congenital leptin deficiency is autosomal recessive; consanguineous healthy parents are the clue.
also: Leptin receptor deficiency is also autosomal recessive, but leptin is high
The first families described were consanguineous
Consanguinity raises the risk of any autosomal recessive disease
Recombinant leptin (metreleptin) treats the deficiency

stem: A 4-day-old girl is lethargic and feeding poorly, with metabolic acidosis and a deficient liver enzyme on assay. Her parents are healthy first cousins. An older sister died at 5 days of age with the same picture, and no other relative is affected.
oneliner: 4-day-old girl + metabolic acidosis, enzyme deficiency + healthy first-cousin parents + older sister died the same way → which inheritance pattern?
ask: Which inheritance pattern is most likely?

whyNot.A: Would show an **affected parent** in each generation; both parents here are **healthy**
whyNot.B: An **affected girl** would need an **affected father** as well as a carrier mother; her father is healthy
whyNot.D: Passes only through the **mother** and is not made likelier by **consanguinity**; a single **liver-enzyme deficiency** with first-cousin parents points to a nuclear recessive gene
whyNot.E: Needs many genes plus environment; a **single-enzyme deficiency** recurring in sisters is a single-gene disorder

why: Two healthy parents with two affected daughters means each parent carries one mutant allele, and each child has a 1/4 chance of being affected. **First-cousin parents** share about 1/8 of their genes, which makes it likely that both carry the same rare allele. Inborn errors that are **enzyme deficiencies** are usually autosomal recessive.

idea.rule: Healthy parents, affected siblings, consanguinity and an enzyme deficiency mean autosomal recessive.
also: PKU and maple syrup urine disease
Homocystinuria (cystathionine synthase deficiency)
Cystic fibrosis
Oculocutaneous albinism
Zellweger syndrome

stem: A 6-month-old girl becomes lethargic and starts vomiting during a viral illness. Ammonia is markedly raised, urine orotic acid is high and plasma citrulline is low. Sequencing shows she is heterozygous for a pathogenic variant in the X-linked ornithine transcarbamylase gene, although most patients with this disease are boys.
oneliner: 6-month-old girl + vomiting, lethargy in viral illness + high ammonia, high orotic acid, low citrulline + heterozygous X-linked OTC variant → why is she symptomatic?
ask: Which mechanism best explains why this heterozygous girl is symptomatic?

options.A: Skewed X inactivation favoring the mutant X in liver
options.B: Genomic imprinting of the gene according to parent of origin
options.C: Uniparental disomy of the X chromosome in her liver cells
options.E: Anticipation from a repeat expansion across generations

whyNot.B: Silences one **parental** copy of an imprinted autosomal gene; she is a **heterozygote for an X-linked gene**, so what matters is which X each liver cell keeps active
whyNot.C: Would need both X copies from one parent; she is a **heterozygote** with one normal and one mutant X
whyNot.D: Concerns the **mitochondrial genome**; the variant is in an **X-linked nuclear gene**
whyNot.E: A feature of **repeat-expansion** disorders that worsen in later generations; she carries a single **pathogenic variant** in a urea cycle gene

answer: Lyonization (skewed X inactivation) favoring the mutant X in hepatocytes
why: **Hyperammonemia with high orotic acid and low citrulline** marks OTC deficiency: carbamoyl phosphate piles up, spills into pyrimidine synthesis (orotic acid up), and little citrulline is made. Each female cell randomly inactivates one X early in development, so a heterozygote is a mosaic; if chance leaves most hepatocytes with the **mutant X active**, OTC activity is low enough to cause disease.

idea.rule: A heterozygous girl with an X-linked recessive disease is symptomatic when X inactivation is skewed against her normal X.
also: Duchenne muscular dystrophy in a carrier girl
Fabry disease in heterozygous women
Hunter syndrome in a rare girl
Lesch-Nyhan syndrome in rare heterozygotes

stem: A 3-year-old boy repeatedly bites his lips and fingers and has writhing limb movements. His mother notices orange crystal-like sand in his diapers, and serum uric acid is high. His parents are healthy, his mother's brother had the same illness, and no female relative is affected.
oneliner: 3M + self-biting, dystonia + orange crystals in diaper, high uric acid + healthy parents, maternal uncle affected, no affected females → which inheritance pattern?
ask: Which inheritance pattern is most likely?

whyNot.A: Would affect **both sexes**; here only a boy and his **maternal uncle** are affected, with no affected females
whyNot.B: Needs an **affected parent** in each generation; his mother and father are healthy
whyNot.C: Heterozygous mothers would be **affected** too; his mother is healthy
whyNot.D: Passes through the mother to sons and daughters alike; **no female relative** is affected

why: **Self-mutilation, dystonia, orange urate crystals and high uric acid** point to HGPRT deficiency, so purines cannot be salvaged and are degraded to uric acid. Affected boys and an **affected maternal uncle**, with a healthy carrier mother and no affected females, fit an **X-linked recessive** pattern.

idea.rule: A healthy carrier mother passes an X-linked recessive disease to sons, so affected maternal uncles are the clue.
also: Duchenne muscular dystrophy
Hemophilia A and B
Bruton X-linked agammaglobulinemia
Hunter syndrome
G6PD deficiency

stem: A 30-year-old man and his unrelated 24-year-old wife seek preconception counseling. His brother has oculocutaneous albinism, an autosomal recessive disease affecting 1 in 40,000 people. The man, his parents and his wife have normal pigmentation, and the wife has no family history. Assume Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium.
oneliner: 30M + brother with albinism (AR, incidence 1 in 40,000) + unaffected parents + unrelated wife with negative family history → risk that their child is affected?
ask: What is the risk that their child will have albinism?

whyNot.A: Treats the man as a **certain** carrier: 1 x 1/100 x 1/4 = 1/400, ignoring that he is unaffected
whyNot.C: Uses a 1/2 chance for the man instead of 2/3: 1/2 x 1/100 x 1/4 = 1/800
whyNot.D: This is the **wife's carrier frequency** (2pq), not the chance her child is affected
whyNot.E: This is the **population incidence** of albinism and ignores the affected brother

why: Incidence q^2 = 1/40,000 gives q = 1/200 and p = 199/200, so the wife's carrier chance is 2pq = 2 x 199/200 x 1/200 = 199/20,000 (about 1/100). The man's parents are both carriers, and he is unaffected, so he is a carrier with probability **2/3**. Risk = 2/3 x 199/20,000 x 1/4 = 398/240,000 = **199/120,000, about 1 in 603**.

idea.rule: Risk to a child = carrier chance of each parent x 1/4, using 2/3 for an unaffected sibling of a patient and 2pq for an unrelated spouse.
also: Unaffected sibling of an AR patient: 2/3 carrier
Carrier frequency 2pq is about 2q when q is small
Child of two known carriers: 1/4 affected
Unaffected child of two carriers: 2/3 carrier

stem: In a genetic association study, 100 healthy control subjects are genotyped at one single-nucleotide polymorphism with alleles A and B. The counts are 30 with AA, 25 with AB and 45 with BB.
oneliner: 100 controls + SNP genotypes AA 30, AB 25, BB 45 → frequency of allele B?
ask: What is the frequency of the B allele in these controls?

whyNot.A: Counts only the **45 BB people**, as if each carried one B; they carry two, and the AB people also contribute
whyNot.B: Counts the **70 people** who carry a B once each (45 + 25) over 200 alleles; BB people carry two B alleles
whyNot.C: Counts only the **BB alleles** (2 x 45), leaving out the B in each of the 25 heterozygotes
whyNot.E: Counts only the **25 heterozygotes** and leaves out the homozygotes

why: Count alleles, not people: 100 people carry **200 alleles**. B alleles = 2 x 45 (BB) + 25 (AB) = **115**, so B frequency = 115/200 = 0.575. Check: A alleles = 2 x 30 + 25 = 85, and 85 + 115 = 200.

idea.rule: Allele frequency = (2 x homozygotes + heterozygotes) / (2 x number of people).
also: Heterozygotes contribute one copy of each allele
Frequencies of the two alleles sum to 1 (0.575 + 0.425)
Hardy-Weinberg expectations use p and q from these counts

stem: A 31-year-old woman and her 33-year-old husband, whose son has a rare autosomal recessive metabolic disease, are told the carrier frequency of the disease. The counselor calculated it from the disease incidence with the Hardy-Weinberg equation, which assumes allele frequencies stay constant across generations.
oneliner: 31F and husband + son with rare AR metabolic disease + carrier frequency estimated from incidence by Hardy-Weinberg → which feature would undermine the estimate?
ask: Which population feature would most undermine this estimate?

options.A: Random mating with respect to genotype
options.C: A high rate of new mutation at the locus
options.D: Equal survival and fertility of all genotypes
options.E: No migration into or out of the population

whyNot.A: Random mating is an **assumption** of the model, so it supports the estimate
whyNot.B: A large population **prevents drift**, as the model requires
whyNot.D: Equal fitness means **no selection**, an assumption that keeps allele frequencies constant
whyNot.E: No gene flow is an **assumption**; it holds allele frequencies steady

answer: A high rate of new mutation at the locus
why: Hardy-Weinberg holds only with **no mutation, no selection, random mating, a large population and no migration**. Frequent new mutation adds mutant alleles each generation, so **allele frequencies change** and the carrier estimate from incidence no longer holds.

idea.rule: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium needs no mutation, no selection, random mating, a large population and no migration.
also: Natural selection against affected homozygotes
Nonrandom (assortative) mating or inbreeding
A small population with genetic drift
Migration that brings in new alleles

stem: A 5-year-old boy has intellectual disability and mild dysmorphic features. His 46,XY karyotype is normal and both parents are healthy. Microsatellite markers across one chromosome region show that both copies came from his mother and none from his father, and methylation testing shows the maternal pattern on both copies.
oneliner: 5M + intellectual disability, mild dysmorphism + normal karyotype + both copies of a region from mother, maternal methylation pattern on both → which mechanism?
ask: Which genetic mechanism best explains his disorder?

whyNot.B: A repeat feature with **earlier, worse disease** in later generations; nothing like that is described
whyNot.C: Passes only through the **mother** to all children and involves mitochondrial DNA; this is a **chromosome region** problem with parent-of-origin methylation
whyNot.D: Needs a **mutant allele from each parent** and a sequence change; here the **methylation pattern** is the abnormal finding
whyNot.E: A mix of normal and mutant **mitochondrial DNA** within a cell; unrelated to chromosome-region parentage

answer: Genomic imprinting (parent-of-origin expression, here with uniparental disomy)
why: A **normal karyotype** with both copies of a region from one parent is **uniparental disomy**, and abnormal **parent-specific methylation** shows that expression depends on the parent of origin. Loss of the normally expressed paternal copy produces disease, which is the hallmark of **genomic imprinting**.

idea.rule: Disease that depends on which parent supplied a chromosome region, with uniparental disomy or abnormal methylation, is an imprinting disorder.
also: Prader-Willi syndrome (paternal 15q11-13 lost)
Angelman syndrome (maternal 15q11-13 lost)
Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome (11p15)
Silver-Russell syndrome

stem: In a population survey, an autosomal recessive disease affects 1 in 1,600 people. A single deletion accounts for 80% of all mutant alleles. Assume Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium.
oneliner: AR disease affects 1 in 1,600 + one deletion = 80% of mutant alleles → frequency of carriers of that deletion?
ask: What is the expected frequency of carriers of the deletion?

whyNot.A: This is the carrier frequency for **all** mutant alleles (78/1,600), before taking the deletion's 80% share
whyNot.B: This is the **allele frequency** q (1/40), not a carrier frequency of the deletion
whyNot.C: This is the deletion's **allele frequency** (0.8 x 1/40 = 0.02), not the carrier frequency, which is about double
whyNot.D: About the **disease frequency** itself, far below any carrier frequency

why: q^2 = 1/1,600 gives q = 1/40 and p = 39/40, so all carriers = 2pq = 2 x 39/40 x 1/40 = 78/1,600 = 0.04875. Deletion carriers = 0.8 x 0.04875 = **0.039**, about **1 in 26** (the nearest simple estimate is 1/25).

idea.rule: Carrier frequency 2pq is about 2q; carriers of one specific mutation = 2pq x its share of mutant alleles.
also: Disease 1 in 10,000 gives q = 1/100 and carriers about 1 in 50
Disease 1 in 40,000 gives carriers about 1 in 100
Cystic fibrosis: disease about 1 in 2,500 gives carriers about 1 in 25
Delta F508 is about 70% of CF mutant alleles in white populations

stem: Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is an X-linked recessive disease affecting 1 in 100,000 males. Assume Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium.
oneliner: X-linked recessive disease affects 1 in 100,000 males → expected frequency of carrier females?
ask: What is the expected frequency of heterozygous (carrier) females?

whyNot.A: This is the **male incidence** (q); carrier females are twice as common
whyNot.C: Halves q instead of doubling it, so it is **four times too low**
whyNot.D: Would need q = 1/20,000; q is **1/100,000**, so this is five times too high
whyNot.E: Treats male incidence as q^2 (q = 0.0032, 2q = 1/158); for X-linked disease, **male incidence equals q**

why: Males have one X, so **male incidence = q = 1/100,000** and p is about 1. Carrier females = 2pq, which is about 2 x 1/100,000 = **2/100,000 = 1/50,000**. Affected females are only q^2 = 1 in 10 billion.

idea.rule: For an X-linked recessive disease, male incidence equals q, carrier females are 2pq (about 2q) and affected females are q^2.
also: Duchenne dystrophy: carrier females are about twice as common as affected males
Hemophilia A: same arithmetic
Autosomal recessive disease differs: incidence is q^2, not q

stem: A pregnant 25-year-old's husband has a fully penetrant autosomal dominant disorder. A DNA marker lies close to the disease gene, with recombination in 10% of meioses. In the husband's family every affected relative carries marker allele 2 and every unaffected relative carries only allele 1. The husband has alleles 1 and 2, his wife has only allele 1, and the fetus has inherited allele 2 from him.
oneliner: 25F pregnant + husband with fully penetrant AD disorder, marker 10% recombination, disease travels with allele 2 + fetus inherited allele 2 → fetal risk?
ask: What is the risk that the fetus has the disorder?

whyNot.A: This is the chance of **recombination**, the risk if the fetus had inherited allele 1 instead
whyNot.B: The **prior risk** before using the marker; the fetus carries the allele that travels with disease
whyNot.C: Implies a 1% recombination fraction; here it is **10%**
whyNot.E: Ignores recombination; with **10% recombination** the marker is not a perfect guide

why: In this family allele 2 is **in phase with the disease allele**. The fetus has the disease allele unless a crossover separated them in the father's meiosis, which happens in 10% of meioses. Risk = 1 - recombination fraction = 1 - 0.10 = **0.90, or 90%**.

idea.rule: A fetus that inherits the marker allele in phase with the disease has risk 1 minus the recombination fraction.
also: The fetus that inherits the other marker allele has risk equal to the recombination fraction (10%)
Tighter linkage gives a more certain answer
Direct mutation testing removes the recombination uncertainty

stem: A 30-year-old woman at 12 weeks' gestation and her 32-year-old husband have a 3-year-old son with cystic fibrosis. Their exact CFTR mutations are unknown, so five polymorphic markers that recombine with CFTR in under 1% of meioses are typed in both parents, the son and the fetus.
oneliner: 30F at 12 weeks + son with cystic fibrosis + CFTR mutations unknown + 5 tightly linked markers typed in parents, son and fetus → which alleles mark the mutant chromosomes?
ask: Which marker alleles should the geneticist treat as lying on each parent's mutant chromosome?

options.A: The alleles the father shares with the mother
options.B: The father's alleles not found in the affected son
options.C: The alleles each parent transmitted to the affected son
options.D: The alleles the fetus received from the mother
options.E: Any allele present in both the son and the fetus, whichever parent gave it

whyNot.A: Shared alleles are **uninformative** because they cannot be assigned to one parent's mutant chromosome
whyNot.B: These sit on the father's **other** chromosome, which the son did not inherit and which is the normal one
whyNot.D: The fetus may have received the **normal** maternal chromosome, so this is circular
whyNot.E: May have come from a **normal** parental chromosome; only alleles traced through the son mark the mutant ones

answer: The alleles each parent passed to the affected son
why: Both parents are obligate carriers of an **autosomal recessive** disease, and the affected son inherited the **mutant chromosome from each**. The marker alleles he received from each parent therefore define the **linkage phase**, and a fetus carrying the same tightly linked alleles from a parent has inherited that mutant chromosome.

idea.rule: In a carrier parent, the marker alleles passed to an affected child mark the mutant chromosome.
also: Phase must be set from the affected child before testing the fetus
Tight linkage keeps recombination under 1%
A fetus with both transmitted sets is affected, with one set a carrier, with none unaffected

stem: A 5-year-old boy has coarse facial features, stiff joints, hepatosplenomegaly and aggressive behavior. Slit-lamp examination shows clear corneas, and urinary glycosaminoglycans are raised. His mother's brother had the same illness, and his sisters are healthy.
oneliner: 5M + coarse facies, stiff joints, hepatosplenomegaly, aggression + clear corneas + high urine GAGs + affected maternal uncle → which disease?
ask: Which lysosomal storage disease is most likely?

whyNot.B: Autosomal recessive with **corneal clouding**; he has **clear corneas** and an affected maternal uncle
whyNot.C: Autosomal recessive; an **affected maternal uncle with healthy sisters** points to X-linked inheritance
whyNot.D: Neurodegeneration without **coarse facies or hepatosplenomegaly**, and autosomal recessive
whyNot.E: Autosomal recessive with organomegaly but **no coarse facies or raised glycosaminoglycans**

why: Coarse facies, stiff joints and hepatosplenomegaly with **raised urinary glycosaminoglycans** mean a mucopolysaccharidosis. **Clear corneas** and an affected **maternal uncle** (X-linked recessive) identify **Hunter syndrome**, whereas Hurler syndrome is autosomal recessive with corneal clouding.

idea.rule: Hunter is the X-linked recessive mucopolysaccharidosis with clear corneas; Hurler is autosomal recessive with clouded corneas.
also: Hunter: iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency, dermatan and heparan sulfate accumulate
Hurler: alpha-L-iduronidase deficiency
Fabry disease: another X-linked lysosomal disease
Hunter has aggressive behavior

stem: A healthy 25-year-old East Asian man develops facial flushing, palpitations and nausea after a single alcoholic drink, and acetaldehyde accumulates in his blood. He is heterozygous for the common E487K variant of aldehyde dehydrogenase 2, an enzyme that works as a tetramer, and his ALDH2 activity is far below 50% of normal.
oneliner: 25M East Asian + flushing, palpitations, nausea after one drink + high acetaldehyde + heterozygous ALDH2 E487K, tetrameric enzyme, activity far below 50% → which effect of the mutation?
ask: Which kind of mutation effect explains his reaction as a heterozygote?

whyNot.A: Half the gene dose would leave **about 50% activity**; his activity is **far below 50%**
whyNot.B: The variant **removes** activity and does not create a new function; acetaldehyde **accumulates**
whyNot.C: Needs loss of the second allele in a cell, as in tumor suppressors; he is **heterozygous**
whyNot.D: Does not change the protein; he has a clear **phenotype** from a missense variant (E487K)

why: The enzyme is a **tetramer**, so one defective subunit poisons the complex. If wild-type and mutant subunits assemble at random, only (1/2)^4 = **1/16 (about 6%)** of tetramers are fully normal, far below the 50% expected from simple loss of one allele, so **heterozygotes already flush**.

idea.rule: In a multimeric protein, a mutant subunit can poison the whole complex (dominant-negative), so heterozygotes are affected.
also: Collagen triple helix mutations in osteogenesis imperfecta
p53 mutations in Li-Fraumeni syndrome
Marfan syndrome (fibrillin-1 multimers)
Dominant-negative mutants of transcription-factor dimers
